chunks: As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā narrated, raising it to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning:
Regarding one who dyes his head with henna and then wishes to perform wudu (ablution), he said: “It is not valid until the water reaches the skin of his head.”

So the correct way of reconciling the two reports is that if it is possible to convey the water to the skin without hardship, then anything else is not permissible; but if that is not possible, it is permissible for him to wipe over the henna. And that which clarifies what we have said is:

key_terms.الْحِنَّاءِ: henna, the substance applied to the head
key_terms.الْخَبَرَيْنِ: the two reports, whose apparent meanings are being reconciled
key_terms.الْمَاءُ: water, required for the validity of wudu (ablution)
key_terms.الْوُضُوءِ: wudu (ablution), the ritual purification being discussed
key_terms.بَشَرَةَ رَأْسِهِ: the skin of his head, which water must reach
key_terms.يَمْسَحَ: to wipe, referring here to wiping over the henna when necessary

ai.seo_question: Can a person perform wudu (ablution) over henna applied to the head?
ai.summary: This passage discusses the ruling of wudu (ablution) for a person who has applied henna to the head. It states that water must reach the skin when possible, but if that becomes unfeasible, wiping over the henna is allowed, showing a juristic reconciliation between reports.
